Culture · Books · Tokyo

Tokyo turned 500 meters of pavement into a million-book treasure hunt.

Jimbocho’s 66th Kanda Used Book Festival opened today with more than 100 wagons. The deeper surprise is that this “temporary” street market rests on a 160-year-old urban machine built around schools.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 23, 2026 at 18:20 JST · 7 min read

On an ordinary day, Yasukuni-dori is a broad central-Tokyo road bordered by buildings whose ground floors seem to speak in categories: old maps here, art books there, modern literature two doors away. Starting today, the shelves have escaped. More than 100 wagons form a roughly 500-meter outdoor “book corridor” through Kanda-Jimbocho.

The organizers call it a one-million-book bargain sale. The 66th Tokyo Famous Kanda Used Book Festival runs from October 23 through November 1, generally from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with a 5 p.m. close on the final day. Rain cancels the outdoor market. The core route follows Yasukuni-dori, although construction at the Iwanami Jimbocho Building has changed part of the usual layout.

1 millionbooks advertised for the festival
100+wagons along the street
500 mthe “book corridor”

The scale is the immediate attraction. The stranger fact is that the festival is not importing a book fair into a picturesque district. It is briefly turning the district inside out. Jimbocho already has roughly 120 to 130 antiquarian booksellers, depending on the official source and counting date. The stock, specialists and buyers are permanent; the wagons merely expose the ecosystem to the weather.

A book town grown from classrooms

Jimbocho’s concentration began around 160 years ago, after the Meiji Restoration, when schools and universities clustered in and around Kanda. Students needed textbooks. Teachers needed specialist works. Authors, printers, publishers, distributors and sellers followed the demand. A neighborhood became a supply chain for knowledge.

That history explains why Jimbocho is not simply a row of charming old shops. Each specialist store functions like a human search engine for a particular slice of paper culture.

The official English map lists fields ranging from academic texts and classical Japanese literature to ukiyo-e, manga, foreign-language books, art and calligraphy. A shopper may arrive with only a remembered cover color or an author’s approximate era. The value of the shop is not merely inventory; it is the proprietor’s ability to locate a clue inside a field that online keywords do not describe well.

At the festival, those separate specialties meet in public. The annual outdoor “treasure hunt” offers the accessible layer. A three-day Special Selection Rare Book Sale at the Tokyo Used Bookstore Hall goes deeper, gathering classical works, handwritten materials and modern first editions. An accompanying free display promises rare books normally seen only in museums and galleries.

The digital age did not remove the hunt

Online catalogs are efficient when a reader knows exactly what to type. The street market works when the reader does not. A spine catches the eye; a neighboring volume changes the question; a price penciled inside a cover reveals how a dealer values condition, edition and scarcity. Discovery is physical and sequential.

That does not make Jimbocho anti-digital. The bookstores publish databases, maps and event information online. Digital search brings buyers to specific stock. The festival’s appeal comes from combining that reach with friction: walking, lifting, comparing, asking and sometimes losing a book to the next person because used inventory is singular.

The official description calls each encounter ichigo ichie—一期一会, a once-in-a-lifetime meeting. Here the phrase is unusually literal. A mass-market title may return tomorrow; an annotated prewar guidebook, discontinued manga volume or small-press first edition may not.

What a visitor can actually do

Jimbocho Station is served by the Tokyo Metro Hanzomon Line and the Toei Mita and Shinjuku lines. The market opens directly into the neighborhood rather than an enclosed ticketed venue. That makes it easy to browse briefly, but the million-book promise rewards a plan: identify one or two subjects, bring a bag that can handle weight, and photograph shop details before moving on.

Visitors who cannot read much Japanese still have routes into the shelves. Art, design, photography, architecture, vintage magazines, maps and manga communicate visually. Some dealers specialize in Western-language books. Asking eigo no hon wa arimasu ka?—“Do you have books in English?”—is more useful than assuming the whole district is inaccessible.

The neighborhood also extends beyond books. Long-running coffee shops and curry restaurants developed alongside the student and publishing population; instrument and sporting-goods districts sit nearby. The festival’s October 24–25 companion events expand into Suzuran-dori and Sakura-dori, while talks and student projects continue on later dates.

The word on every shop sign

Today’s book-district word is 古本, furuhon: a used or secondhand book. 古 means old; 本 means book. In ordinary speech and shop signs it is broader and friendlier than imagining only museum-grade antiquarian volumes. A 古本屋 (furuhonya) is a used-book shop; 古書 (kosho) often carries a more antiquarian or specialist shade.

The distinction fits Jimbocho. A 200-yen paperback and a rare handwritten document can exist within the same urban system, but they invite different kinds of attention. One is a cheap next read. The other may be an artifact with provenance, marginalia and material history.

The festival matters today because it makes that continuum visible. A city associated with screens, convenience and constant replacement closes no futuristic loop here. It puts old paper on more than 100 carts and trusts that people will stop. For ten days, Tokyo’s most remarkable search interface is half a kilometer long and operated by booksellers.
